name: Dead Sea Scrolls
info: Ancient Jewish manuscripts of the Second Temple period, dated from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE and found in caves near Qumran between 1946 and 1956, including the oldest surviving copies of biblical books.

facts.made: Jewish scribes of the Second Temple period; long associated with the Essenes at Khirbet Qumran, though some scholars attribute them to Sadducee priests, Jerusalem libraries or other Jewish groups
facts.form: About 15,000 scrolls and fragments from 981 manuscripts, mostly in Hebrew, some in Aramaic and Greek; written mainly on parchment, some on papyrus and one on copper
facts.where: Almost all in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem; part of the collection, with the Copper Scroll, at The Jordan Museum in Amman
facts.known: The Great Isaiah Scroll; the oldest manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible; the Community Rule and War Scroll; the Qumran–Essene hypothesis; Cave 4's 15,000 fragments; the long delays in publication; disputed ownership

t: The scrolls pushed the oldest known Hebrew biblical manuscripts back more than a millennium and showed both the stability of the Masoretic tradition and a fluid text before about 100 CE.
About 40% are copies of canonical scriptures, about 30% other Second Temple texts such as Enoch and Jubilees, and the rest sectarian works such as the Community Rule.
Who wrote them is debated: the Qumran–Essene theory held almost universally until the 1990s is now challenged by Sadducee, Jerusalem and other origins.
dyk: The Temple Scroll from Cave 11, by far the longest, measures 8.15 metres, and its original length may have been over 8.75 metres.
ev: Bedouin shepherds found the first seven scrolls in jars in what became Cave 1, between November 1946 and February 1947
Millar Burrows of the American Schools of Oriental Research announced the discovery
Cave 4, by far the most productive of the caves, was found and excavated
Four scrolls advertised in The Wall Street Journal were bought for Israel for $250,000
Cave 11 yielded the last fragments found near Qumran, among them the Temple Scroll
The collection moved to the newly built Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem
A Facsimile Edition and the opening of the Huntington Library's photographs ended restricted access
The 40th and final volume of Discoveries in the Judaean Desert was published

sections.origins:
The scrolls come from the late Second Temple period of Jewish history. Scholarly consensus dates them between the 3rd century BCE and the 1st century CE, and bronze coins found at the same sites run from John Hyrcanus, ruler of Hasmonean Judea from 135 to 104 BCE, to the First Jewish–Roman War of 66 to 73 CE. The eleven Qumran caves lie near Khirbet Qumran, a Hellenistic-period Jewish settlement about 1.5 kilometres from the north-western shore of the Dead Sea. Storing worn-out sacred manuscripts in jars or caves is related to the ancient Jewish custom of genizah.

Who produced them is much debated. The Qumran–Essene hypothesis of Roland de Vaux and Józef Milik, almost universally held until the 1990s, points to likenesses between the Community Rule and Josephus's account of the Essenes, inkwells in a room de Vaux called the scriptorium, ritual baths, and Pliny the Elder's report of Essenes near the Dead Sea. Lawrence Schiffman has argued for Zadokite priests, citing the purity laws of 4QMMT. Karl Heinrich Rengstorf and Norman Golb proposed libraries in Jerusalem, and some archaeologists see Qumran as a Hasmonean fort.
sections.content:
Researchers have assembled 981 manuscripts from 11 caves. About 40% are copies of texts from the Hebrew scriptures; there are parts of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, and of Tobit, Sirach, Baruch 6 and Psalm 151. About 30% are Second Temple texts that were not canonised, such as the Book of Enoch, Jubilees and Psalms 152 to 155. The rest are previously unknown sectarian works that describe the rules and beliefs of a group within Judaism, such as the Community Rule, the War Scroll, the Pesher on Habakkuk and the Rule of the Blessing.

Cave 1 held the original seven scrolls: the Great Isaiah Scroll, a second copy of Isaiah, the Community Rule, the Pesher on Habakkuk, the War Scroll, the Thanksgiving Hymns and the Genesis Apocryphon. Cave 4 produced about 90% of the material, some 15,000 fragments from 500 texts, with tefillin and mezuzot. Cave 3 gave the Copper Scroll, and Cave 11 the Temple Scroll, which Yigael Yadin called "The Torah According to the Essenes" and Hartmut Stegemann thought of no exceptional significance. Most texts are in Hebrew, some in Aramaic and a few in Greek.
sections.making:
Most texts are written on parchment made from animal hide, about 85.5 to 90.5% of the scrolls, with papyrus making up 8 to 13% and sheets of copper and tin about 1.5%. Tests in Sicily on water used in the parchment suggested that some of it was made in the Qumran area. DNA testing by the Israel Antiquities Authority suggests a possible hierarchy of importance, with goat and calf hide used for more significant texts than gazelle or ibex.

The black ink is carbon black, mostly soot from olive oil lamps, thinned with honey, oil, vinegar and water and sometimes strengthened with galls; a red ink of cinnabar occurs only four times. The writers used reed pens. Palaeographers such as Cross and Avigad dated fragments from 225 BCE to 50 CE by their letter forms. Radiocarbon tests, first on linen in 1950, gave VanderKam and Flint "strong reason" to place most manuscripts in the last two centuries BCE and the 1st century CE. A study of 2025 led by Mladen Popović, using radiocarbon dates and an AI model called Enoch, proposed older dates for some, placing a Daniel fragment between 230 and 160 BCE.
sections.reception:
John C. Trever of the American Schools of Oriental Research compared the script of the first scrolls with the Nash Papyrus, then the oldest known biblical manuscript, and the discovery was announced in April 1948. For scholars of the Hebrew Bible the central question was whether the scrolls would confirm or undermine the Masoretic text, whose oldest manuscripts dated from about the 9th and 10th centuries CE. Millar Burrows stressed their agreement with the Masoretic tradition; Paul Kahle stressed the variant readings, and Burrows came to accept them as the second point of importance.

Manuscripts of Exodus and Samuel from Cave 4 differ greatly from the traditional text, leading scholars to rethink the theory of three manuscript families. Interpreters have read the scrolls in many ways: José O'Callaghan argued that fragment 7Q5 preserves Mark 6:52–53, and Robert Eisenman linked some texts to the early Christian community. Publication was slow, controlled by a small editorial team headed by John Strugnell, and scholars such as Norman Golb and the writer Hershel Shanks campaigned for decades for open access, which came in 1991.
sections.survival:
The dry climate, untanned parchment, low airflow in the caves and storage in clay jars preserved the scrolls. After discovery they deteriorated faster: adhesive tape damaged them in the late 1940s and early 1950s, fragments lay between window glass at the Palestine Archaeological Museum in East Jerusalem, and storage in a damp bank vault in Amman during the Suez Crisis brought mildew. By 1958 up to 5% of some scrolls had perished. In 1991 the Israel Antiquities Authority set up a climate-controlled laboratory.

Najib Albina's infrared photographs of 1952 to 1967 are often considered the best record of the fragments before further decay. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory applied multispectral imaging from 1993, and the Israel Museum and Google put high-resolution images online from 2011. Ownership is contested: the scrolls were mostly found after the Jordanian annexation of the West Bank and came under Israeli control after the 1967 war, and Jordan and the Palestinian Authority dispute Israel's custody, while Israel's claim rests on historical and religious grounds. Forgeries have appeared since 2002; in 2020 the Museum of the Bible found all 16 of its fragments to be modern fakes.
sections.legacy:
The scrolls cast new light on the emergence of Rabbinic Judaism and of Christianity. They showed that the Masoretic tradition was transmitted with remarkable overall stability from the 2nd century BCE, while revealing a fluid biblical text before its standardisation around 100 CE. Scholars now also recognise that some non-biblical works were composed earlier than the community that kept them, while some biblical books were still being written or edited.

Their publication shaped scholarship and law. The 40 volumes of Discoveries in the Judaean Desert appeared from Oxford University Press between 1955 and 2009, accelerated under Emanuel Tov from 1990. The case of Qimron v. Shanks, decided for Elisha Qimron in 1993 and upheld by Israel's Supreme Court in 2000, held that a scholar's deciphered text can be protected by copyright while the scrolls themselves are not. The Shrine of the Book has displayed them since 1965, and searches in the Judaean Desert still yield finds, such as a twelfth cave in 2017 and Greek fragments of Zechariah and Nahum in 2021, and the project Tracing Scribes and Scrolls, announced in 2026, is studying 250 items with artificial intelligence.

summary: The Dead Sea Scrolls are some 15,000 fragments of Jewish manuscripts from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE, found near Qumran between 1946 and 1956. They include the oldest surviving copies of biblical books and previously unknown sectarian texts, whose authors are debated, and their custody remains disputed between Israel, Jordan and the Palestinian Authority.
